title: Embeddings in practice: model choice, dimensions, cost
story:
The coordinates in an embedding have no meaning of their own. They are positions relative to everything else the model placed, which makes the space a product of one model rather than a description of the text. Two models given the same sentence produce two sets of numbers, and comparing across them is not a worse comparison — it is not a comparison at all.

Every practical consequence in this lesson comes from that one fact, so it is worth stating in the form you will actually need it: the choice of embedding model is not a setting. It is a commitment to a migration.

Changing the model means re-embedding every document you hold, rebuilding the index, and living with a period during which the store contains vectors from two spaces. That period is where the danger is, because a mixed store does not fail loudly. Nothing raises an error. Distances still come back, still look like numbers, still rank. They simply mean nothing, and the system returns confident nonsense in the shape of results.

So record which model and which version produced each vector, store it beside the vector, and refuse at write time to put a foreign one in. A failure you cannot detect will be found eventually by a user, and this one is invisible from the outside, which is the worst combination there is.

The width of the vector is the second decision and it behaves differently: it is a price rather than a commitment. Every item you store pays it, in storage, in memory, and in the work done by every comparison — so the width multiplies by the size of the corpus and then by the rate of queries, and it is paid for as long as the system exists. A narrower vector halves that bill straightforwardly. What it costs you in quality is not knowable from the number, only from measurement on your own data, and a wider vector is not automatically a better one.

Which brings up how to choose at all. A public ranking of models is a real measurement of somebody else's corpus and somebody else's questions. Yours has its own vocabulary, its identifiers and part numbers and internal abbreviations, and a distribution of questions you could write down in an afternoon. Take twenty real questions with the passages that ought to answer them, run each candidate model against that set, and you will have a better basis for the decision than any ranking, along with a test you can re-run the next time somebody proposes a change.

The cost of embedding has two sides, and only one of them is usually noticed. Documents are embedded once, plus again whenever they change, which is a batch job you can schedule and make cheap. Queries are embedded on every single request, which puts that call inside your request path forever. The model you choose is therefore a latency decision as much as a quality one, and a model that is marginally better and noticeably slower is being paid for by every user on every question.

A last practical matter, because it is the quiet failure that catches people who have done everything else right. Models have a limit on how much text they will take, and what happens past that limit is often silent truncation. A long document goes in, a vector comes out, everything looks normal, and the second half of the document was never read. Know your model's limit, know what it does when it is exceeded, and check rather than assume — a system that discards half your corpus without saying so will keep working just well enough that nobody investigates.

problem.name: Committing to a vector space
problem.shape: A stored representation is only meaningful relative to the model that produced it, and it has to be paid for on every item and every query.
tell: someone proposes swapping the embedding model as a configuration change
vectors from more than one model are in the same store
the model was chosen from a public ranking rather than from your own questions
documents longer than the model's limit are being embedded without checking what happens to the remainder
problem.move: Treat the model choice as a migration: record the model and version beside every vector, refuse mixed writes, and keep a re-embedding job you can run on purpose. Choose by measuring candidates against your own questions, and size the vector knowing you pay for its width on every item and every comparison.
problem.invariant: Distances are only meaningful within one space produced by one model, so every vector compared must come from the same model and version.
problem.breaks: A mixed store fails silently — no error is raised, distances still rank, and the results are meaningless — and text past the model's input limit is often dropped without any signal.

cost.time: documents are embedded once and queries on every request, so the query-side call sits in the request path permanently
cost.space: the vector width is paid per item and multiplied by the size of the corpus, in storage, in memory and in every comparison
cost.beats: keyword indexes, which are cheaper and cannot match meaning, and calling a model to judge relevance directly, which is far too slow to run over a corpus

problem.practice: Embed a document that is comfortably longer than your model's stated limit, then embed only its first half, and compare the two vectors. If they are identical or nearly so, you have just watched your pipeline throw away the second half without telling you, and you will never again assume that step is safe.

beats.broke: Vectors are positions in a space owned by one model, so anything that treats the model as a swappable setting produces a store whose distances are meaningless.
beats.fix: Treat the model as a migration commitment — record model and version with every vector, refuse mixed writes, keep a re-embedding job — and choose by measuring candidates on your own questions.
beats.cost: The width is paid on every item and every comparison for the life of the system, and the query-side embedding call sits inside every request.

interview.q: What are you committing to when you pick an embedding model, and what does the vector width actually cost?
interview.trap: Assuming a mixed store will error. It will not — distances still rank and still look like numbers, so the failure is invisible from outside and shows up as confident nonsense.
interview.answer:
To a migration. The coordinates have no meaning on their own; they are positions relative to everything else that model placed, so the space belongs to the model and vectors from two models are not comparable at all. Changing the model means re-embedding every document, rebuilding the index, and passing through a window where the store holds two spaces.

That window is what I plan for, because a mixed store does not fail loudly. No error is raised, distances still come back and still rank, and they mean nothing — confident nonsense in the shape of results. So I store the model and version beside every vector and refuse foreign writes at write time.

The width is a price rather than a commitment: paid per item in storage and memory, and per comparison in work, multiplied by corpus size and query rate for the life of the system. Narrower halves the bill; what it costs in quality is only knowable by measuring on my own data, and wider is not automatically better.

On choosing between models, a public ranking measures someone else's corpus and questions. I would rather take twenty real questions with the passages that should answer them and run every candidate against that, which gives me both the decision and a regression test for the next proposed change.

And I would separate the two costs: documents are embedded once in a batch job, queries on every request — so the model choice is a latency decision that every user pays. The quiet failure to check for is the input limit, where exceeding it often means silent truncation and a perfectly normal-looking vector for a document whose second half was never read.
